title: If Statements and Operators
summary: Make decisions with if, comparison operators, the logical operators &&, ||, and !, and String equals.
intro: Programs get interesting when they make decisions. In Java that starts with comparisons that produce `true` or `false`, and an `if` that runs code only when its condition is `true`.

steps.title: Comparisons and if

example.title: Ages and temperatures
example.prompt: Compare the ages 15 and 18 with every operator, show the two double gotchas, then check the temperatures 34 and -3, printing hot only above 30 and freezing only below 0.
example.output:
age == adultAge: false
age != adultAge: true
age < adultAge: true
age > adultAge: false
age <= adultAge: true
age >= adultAge: false
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3: false
nan == nan: false
Double.isNaN(nan): true
34 is hot
-3 is freezing
example.explanation: Each comparison is in parentheses, so it becomes `true` or `false` before `+` joins it to the label. `0.1 + 0.2` is really `0.30000000000000004`, so `==` says `false`, and `nan == nan` is `false` while `Double.isNaN` gives the right answer. For 34 the first `if` is true and the second is false, so only the hot line prints. After `temperature` is reassigned to -3, the same two checks run again and this time only the freezing line prints.

practice.title: Score check
practice.prompt:
Compare a score of 72 with a goal of 100, then check the scores 72 and 100 with two if statements.

1. Print `score >= 50: ` followed by the result of `score >= 50`.
2. Print `score == goal: ` followed by the result of `score == goal`.
3. Print `score < goal: ` followed by the result of `score < goal`.
4. Print `72 passed`, using the real score, only if `score >= 50`.
5. Print `72 is perfect`, using the real score, only if `score == goal`.
6. Set `score` to `100` and repeat the two if statements.

Expected output:

```text
score >= 50: true
score == goal: false
score < goal: true
72 passed
100 passed
100 is perfect
```

tests.output:
score >= 50: true
score == goal: false
score < goal: true
72 passed
100 passed
100 is perfect

hints: Put each comparison in parentheses before joining it with the label: `"score >= 50: " + (score >= 50)`.
Write two separate `if` statements with braces. For 72 only the first condition is true, and for 100 both are.

steps.title: Logical operators
steps.body:
Combine booleans with three logical operators:

- `a && b` (and) is `true` only when both sides are `true`.
- `a || b` (or) is `true` when at least one side is `true`.
- `!a` (not) flips `true` to `false` and back.

A range check needs both ends written out. Java has no `1 <= x <= 10`, so write `x >= 1 && x <= 10`.

```java
int x = 7;
System.out.println(x >= 1 && x <= 10); // true
System.out.println(!(x > 5));          // false
```

Put a comparison in parentheses before negating it: `!x > 5` does not compile. Also, `&&` binds tighter than `||`, so add parentheses when you mix them.

`&&` and `||` short-circuit: they stop as soon as the answer is known. If the left side of `&&` is `false`, the right side never runs. If the left side of `||` is `true`, the right side is skipped too. That makes `d != 0 && n / d > 2` safe when `d` is 0, because the division that would throw an `ArithmeticException` is skipped. Use the doubled forms: a single `&` or `|` also works on booleans but always runs both sides.

example.title: Ticket rules
example.prompt: Check ticket rules for a 70 year old non-member with &&, ||, and !, run the child range check again for an 8 year old, then guard a division by zero with short-circuit evaluation.
example.output:
Child ticket: false
Discount: true
Allowed in: true
Senior ticket printed
Child ticket: true
Ratio above 2: false
example.explanation: 70 fails the range check `age >= 3 && age <= 12`, so Child ticket is false. `isMember` is false but `age >= 65` is true, so the `||` gives true. `!isBanned` flips false to true, and both sides of the `if` are true, so its line prints. After `age` becomes 8, the same range check is true. Last, `d != 0` is false, so `&&` stops there and never divides by zero.

practice.title: Store hours
practice.prompt:
Decide whether a store is open at hour 18 and then hour 10 on a normal day and whether a customer gets a discount.

1. Use the variables in the starter: `hour` is 18, `isHoliday` is false, `isStudent` is true, `isSenior` is false.
2. Print `Open: ` followed by whether `hour` is from 9 to 17 inclusive and it is not a holiday.
3. Print `Discount: ` followed by whether the customer is a student or a senior.
4. Set `hour` to `10` and print the `Open: ` line again.

Expected output:

```text
Open: false
Discount: true
Open: true
```

tests.output:
Open: false
Discount: true
Open: true

hints: Open needs three things to be true at once, so join them with `&&`.
Use `!isHoliday` for not a holiday, and wrap the whole condition in parentheses inside the concatenation.

steps.title: Boolean flags, null checks, and equals

example.title: Weather advice
example.prompt: Print advice from two weather flags, first while it rains and then when it stops, print a nickname only when it is not null, then print Starting only when a command equals start, checking a null command and then a start command.
example.output:
Stay inside
Go for a walk
Nickname: Ace
Command: null
Command: start
Starting
example.explanation: It is raining and there is no umbrella, so only `isRaining && !hasUmbrella` is true. Once `isRaining` is false, the same three checks run again and only `!isRaining` is true. The first nickname check skips its block because `nickname` is `null`, and after it becomes `"Ace"` the same check passes. For the `null` command, `command != null` is false, so `&&` stops before `equals` could crash. The second check puts the literal first: `"start".equals(command)` compares the text and is simply `false` for `null`, so both forms are safe.

practice.title: Morning plan
practice.prompt:
Decide what to do on two mornings, then apply a coupon only when it is valid.

1. Print `Turn off the alarm` if `isWeekend` and `isAlarmSet` are both true.
2. Print `Sleep in` if `isWeekend` is true and `isAlarmSet` is false.
3. Print `Go to work` if `isWeekend` is false.
4. Set `isWeekend` to `false` and run the same three checks again.
5. After each `Coupon:` line in the starter, print `Discount applied` only if `coupon` is not null and equals `SAVE10`. Compare the text with `equals`, never `==`, in a way that cannot crash on `null`.

Expected output:

```text
Turn off the alarm
Go to work
Coupon: null
Coupon: SAVE10
Discount applied
```

tests.output:
Turn off the alarm
Go to work
Coupon: null
Coupon: SAVE10
Discount applied

hints: Use each flag directly as a condition, and put `!` in front when a flag must be false.
Write `coupon != null && coupon.equals("SAVE10")` so `equals` never runs on `null`. `"SAVE10".equals(coupon)` works too.

recap:
- `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` produce a `boolean`. Wrap them in parentheses inside a concatenation.
- `if (condition) { ... }` runs its block only when the condition is `true`. Always use braces.
- Never compare doubles with `==`, and test `NaN` with `Double.isNaN`.
- `&&` is and, `||` is or, `!` is not. `&&` and `||` short-circuit, so `d != 0 && n / d > 2` is safe.
- Range checks spell out both ends: `x >= 1 && x <= 10`.
- Use a `boolean` flag directly: `if (isReady)`.
- Compare String text with `equals`, never `==`. Guard with `s != null && s.equals("text")` or write `"text".equals(s)`.
